sentence: ___ na mákit mɔ́!
translation: ‘Pass by the market again!’
knowledge_point: The two other combinations of verb negation and a clause-final adverbial are nó -- mɔ́ ‘no more, not again’ and nó -- sɛ́f ‘not even’. Compare the affirmative use of mɔ́ ‘more’ in \REF{ex:key:538} with \REF{ex:key:545} below.

sentence: A kán ___ ínsay hós.
translation: ‘(Then) I hid in the house.’
knowledge_point: The basic posture verbs slíp ‘lie (down), sleep’, tínap ‘stand (up)’ and sidɔ́n ‘sit (down)’ are never encountered with a reflexive pronoun in the corpus (cf. \sectref{sec:8.1.3} for an extensive treatment). In contrast, verbs denoting less prototypical postures, e.g. líng ‘lean over’ and bɛ́n ‘bend (over)’ in (\ref{ex:key:1303}–\ref{ex:key:1304}), as well as those denoting other types of body-related events, e.g. the morpheme ___ ‘its gloss ___’ in (\ref{ex:key:1305}–\ref{ex:key:1306}) are found with or without reflexive pronouns:

sentence: Wé di bɔ́y in ___ wé e sí mí, estaba contento.
gloss: SUB DEF boy 3SG.POSS ___ SUB 3SG.SBJ see 1SG.INDP he.was content
translation: ‘And the boy himself, when he saw me, he was content.’
knowledge_point: The construction in \REF{ex:key:664} is, however, marginal. Note the difference between \REF{ex:key:664} and the following \REF{ex:key:665}. In the latter example, the morpheme ___ ‘its gloss ___, \textsc{emp}’ is used as a regular focus particle, postposed to the high-toned \textsc{3sg} emphatic personal pronoun:

sentence: A ___ smɛ́l di sɛ́nt fɔ lɛk háw e de kúk plantí.
gloss: 1SG.SBJ ___ smell DEF scent PREP like how 3SG.SBJ IPFV cook plantain
translation: ‘I smell the scent of him cooking plantain.’
knowledge_point: Present tense\is{present tense} is not expressed by means of elements specialised to this function. Instead, present tense reference is established by the morpheme ___fault through a variety of means. Bare stative verbs (cf. \ref{ex:key:315}) and in the appropriate context inchoative-stative verbs \REF{ex:key:316} are assigned present tense by the morpheme ___fault when marked for factative\is{factative TMA} TMA. Present tense reference is also established with inchoative-stative verbs via the use of the imperfective aspec\is{imperfective aspect}t marker the morpheme ___ (cf. \ref{ex:key:336}) and with both lexical aspect classes by the use of the habitual\is{habitual aspect} marker kin (cf. \ref{ex:key:344}–\ref{ex:key:345}). Dynamic verbs are assigned present tense by the morpheme ___fault when they appear with the imperfective marker the morpheme ___ (cf. \ref{ex:key:329}) and the habitual aspect marker kin (cf. \ref{ex:key:342}).

sentence: Pero bambáy bambáy ___ yu go sí di wán wé go máred yú.
gloss: but gradually REP ___ 2SG POT see DEF one SUB POT marry 2SG.INDP
translation: ‘But very gradually perhaps you might find the one who will marry you.’
knowledge_point: The two modal adverbs the morpheme ___ ‘its gloss ___’ (cf. \ref{ex:key:840} above) and smɔ́ltɛn ‘nearly’ \REF{ex:key:848} and the evaluative adverb bádtɛn ‘unfortunately’ \REF{ex:key:847} are lexicalised phrases involving the generic noun tɛ́n ‘time’ as a formative element (cf. \ref{ex:key:103} above). Modal and evaluative adverbs are normally found in the initial position with scope over the entire clause:

sentence: E wás dí klós dɛn, e dráy dɛ́n, nɔ́ na ___ dráy dɛ́n.
gloss: 3SG.SBJ wash this clothing PL 3SG.SBJ dry 3PL.INDP INTJ FOC ___ dry 3PL.INDP
translation: ‘She washed the clothes, she dried them, no, it is me (who) dried them.’
knowledge_point: Likewise, only independent personal pronouns occur under focus in cleft constructions {\fff}involving the focus markers na ‘\textsc{foc}’ \REF{ex:key:281}, and nóto ‘\textsc{neg.foc}’. The example also shows the use of independent pronouns (i.e. dɛ́n ‘\textsc{3pl.indp}’) as regular object pronouns (save the clitic =an for \textsc{3sg.obj}):

sentence: Na ___ ús=tín dɛn ték bíl di hós?
gloss: FOC ___ Q=thing 3PL take build DEF house
translation: ‘With what did they build the house?’
knowledge_point: Secondly, we find double marking of the instrument objects of ték ‘take’ as a rather regular way of questioning these objects. In \REF{ex:key:611}, the object of ték (i.e. ús=tín ‘what’) is fronted and focused. The question word and object ús=tín is additionally preceded by the instrumental/comitative preposition the morpheme ___ ‘its gloss ___’ as if the corresponding declarative clause had been something ungrammatical like *dɛn ték the morpheme ___ plɛ́nk bíl di hós ‘\textsc{3pl} take its gloss ___ board build \textsc{def} house’ = *‘they took its gloss ___ board to build the house’ (cf. also \ref{ex:key:1571}–\ref{ex:key:1572}):

sentence: E pás ___ mí.
translation: ‘He went past next to me.’
knowledge_point: The locative nouns nía ‘near’, the morpheme ___ ‘next to’, nadó ‘outside’, and bifó ‘before, front’ are not normally found as complements to na ‘\textsc{loc}’ in prepositional phrases\is{prepositional phrases} like the ones above. The peculiar distribution of nía and the morpheme ___ may be due to their multifunctionality. Nía also functions as a locative verb ‘be near’ (cf. \ref{ex:key:939}), the morpheme ___ as a common noun ‘corner’, and bifó as a time clause linker ‘before’ (cf. \sectref{sec:10.7.3}). In \REF{ex:key:933} below, the morpheme ___ is employed as a locative noun, in the following example \REF{ex:key:916}, as a common noun:

sentence: Na frɔn in hós, ___ dé yu go ték máred.
gloss: FOC from 3SG.POSS house ___ there 2SG POT take marry
translation: ‘It’s from her house, it’s there that you’d enter marriage.’
knowledge_point: In \REF{ex:key:717}, the topical, clefted adverbial phrase frɔn in hós ‘from her house’ is athe morpheme ___phorically referred to by another clefted adverbial, the morpheme ___mely dé ‘there’:

sentence: \'{A}fta yu fɔ ___ dɛ́n.
translation: ‘Then you have to pay them.’
knowledge_point: Impersonalised purposive\is{purpose clauses} constructions like \REF{ex:key:417} are likely to be one point of departure for the occurrence of fɔ as a mood marker in finite clauses like \REF{ex:key:418}. The various uses of fɔ as a clause linker form part of a web of interrelated functions of this element (cf. \sectref{sec:10.2} for an overview):

sentence: Dɛn chák di ___ fɔ́s fɔ mék dɛn fít gó tíf.
gloss: 3PL get.drunk DEF ___ first PREP SBJV 3PL can go steal
translation: ‘They got the guard drunk first in order for them to be able to steal.’
knowledge_point: At the same time, the aspectual reading of the bare factative change of state verb is adjusted. When the verb is employed as a bare inchoative-stative verb in a basic intransitive clause, as in \REF{ex:key:1110} below, it normally receives a present tense\is{present tense} interpretation – the situation holds at reference time. In turn, the dynamic variant of chák receives a default past tense\is{past tense} interpretation in \REF{ex:key:1111}.

sentence: \textstylePichiglossZchn{Yú} ___ de gó?
translation: ‘You want to (get) go(ing)?’
knowledge_point: The manipulative verb of desire wánt ‘its gloss ___’ is very versatile. It may occur in same subject\is{subjects} complement clauses (cf. e.g. \ref{ex:key:412}) or may take complements featuring the imperfective marker de ‘\textsc{ipfv}’ (cf. e.g. \ref{ex:key:1381}). When the subjects of the main and complement clauses are not the same, a subjunctive mék{}-complement is required:

sentence: Dán skúl, ___ dé nía bɛrin-grɔ́n, nɔ́?
gloss: that school ___ BE.LOC near burial.CPD-ground INTJ
translation: ‘That school is near the cemetery, right?’

At ththe morpheme ___ samthe morpheme ___ timthe morpheme ___, ththe morpheme ___ following corthe morpheme ___fthe morpheme ___rthe morpheme ___ntial rthe morpheme ___sumptivthe morpheme ___ pronoun\is{rthe morpheme ___sumptivthe morpheme ___ pronouns} the morpheme ___ ‘\tthe morpheme ___xtsc{3sg.sbj}’ rthe morpheme ___itthe morpheme ___ratthe morpheme ___s ththe morpheme ___ topical subjthe morpheme ___ct \tthe morpheme ___xtsc{NP} dán skúl ‘that school’:

sentence: A bin ___ máred a los veinti-uno ɛf Maura in papa nó bin dáy.
gloss: 1SG.SBJ PST ___ marry at DEF.PL twenty-one if NAME 3SG.POSS father NEG PST die
translation: ‘I should/would have married at twenty-one if Maura’s father hadn’t died.’
knowledge_point: In the vast majority of cases, the \textsc{if-}clause precedes the \textsc{then-}clause in Pichi conditionals. Nevertheless, the corpus contains a few instances of initial \textsc{then-}clauses \REF{ex:key:1533}. These types of conditionals are pragmatically marked and usually involve focus of the preposed \textsc{then-}clause. This example is also of interest, because it reflects some of the residual obligation meaning that the preposition cum modal particle the morpheme ___ may have in counterfactual conditionals (cf. also \sectref{sec:6.7.3.2}):

sentence: Lúk=an, di dé wé dís Paquita in papá bin kán ___ e pé avioneta kɔmɔ́t Alemania, rích na Douala, pé avioneta, e kán na yá só.
gloss: look=3SG.OBJ DEF day SUB this NAME 3SG.POSS father PST come ___ 3SG.SBJ pay small.aircraft go.out PLACE reach LOC PLACE pay small.aircraft 3SG.SBJ come LOC here like.that
translation: ‘Look at her, the day that Paquita’s father came to take her, he paid (a ticket for) a small plane, left Germany, got to Douala, paid (a ticket for) a small plane, (and) came here.’
knowledge_point: The following example illustrates how the difference between clause chaining and the linkage of fully finite clauses may hinge on intonation when a series of dynamic verbs are marked for factative TMA.\is{resumptive pronouns} In \REF{ex:key:1612}, the verbs ték ‘take’, pé ‘pay’, kɔmɔ́t ‘go out’, rích ‘arrive’, and pé ‘pay’ are iconically ordered along the time axis and describe successive events. However, they are separated by pauses. Additionally, the last constituent of each clause bears continuative intonation\is{continuative intonation} (indicated by a comma), which alerts the hearer to the existence of a clausal boundary. For these reasons, \REF{ex:key:1612} does not involve clause chaining:

sentence: A de hía ín sé e de nák di gitá ɔ a de hía ín ___ háw e de nák di gita.
gloss: 1SG.SBJ IPFV hear 3SG.INDP QUOT 3SG.SBJ IPFV hit DEF guitar or 1SG.SBJ IPFV hear 3SG.INDP ___ how 3SG.SBJ IPFV hit DEF guitar
translation: ‘I hear him that he’s playing the guitar.’ or ‘I hear him how he’s playing the guitar.’
knowledge_point: The disjunctive coordinator ɔ ‘or’ may also link coordinate clauses, cf. \REF{ex:key:1408} for an example.

sentence: Mí wet Rubi wi mék ___ wi báy pía, wi báy sadín, wi báy tomates, wi desayuna.
gloss: 1SG.INDP with NAME 1PL make ___ 1PL buy avocado 1PL buy sardine 1PL buy tomatoes 1PL breakfast
translation: ‘Me and Rubi, we joined up, we bought avocados, we bought sardines, we bought tomatoes, we had breakfast.’
knowledge_point: Further, the interaction of verbal and nominal plurality often characterises the use of iterative aspect. The presence of plural referents generally induces a sense of iterative-distributive action of the situation denoted by the verb. For example, the light verb construction in \REF{ex:key:140} features the reduplicated nominalised verb jwɛ́n ‘join’. The presence of the plural subject mí wet Rubi ‘me and Rubi’, which is picked up by the resumptive pronoun{\fff} wi ‘\textsc{1pl}’, induces a cumulative meaning of the reduplicated and deverbal noun jwɛ́n ‘join’:

sentence: A tɛ́l ___ dɛn nó lɛ́k pɔ́sin.
translation: ‘I tell you, they don’t like people.’
knowledge_point: Other phrasal interjections are employed to seek attention, approbation and confirmation. The phrases nó tɔ́k ‘don’t talk’, which appears together with nɔ́ and ɛ́n in \REF{ex:key:655} further above, and nó láf ‘\textsc{neg} laugh’ = ‘I’m not kidding’ \REF{ex:key:1660b} underline the credibility of the speaker’s proposition or story. A similar function is fulfilled by a tɛ́l the morpheme ___ ‘I tell you’ in \REF{ex:key:1661}:

sentence: E dɔ́n sté, a tínk sé e dɔ́n sté ___ una bin gɛ́t insecticida yá.
gloss: 3SG.SBJ PRF be.long 1SG.SBJ think QUOT 3SG.SBJ PRF be.long ___ 2PL PST get insecticide here
translation: ‘It’s long ago, I think that it’s long ago that you people had insecticide here/when you people last had insecticide here.’
knowledge_point: The the morpheme ___-clause in \REF{ex:key:1412} is a borderline case that may either be analysed as an adverbial clause, i.e. a modifying time clause, or a subject complement clause:

sentence: Dís wán sɛ́f, yu dɔ́n ___ tráy.
translation: ‘Even this [little Bube that you speak], you’re really making an effort.’
knowledge_point: In \REF{ex:key:742}, NP focus (i.e. dís wán sɛ́f ‘this one \textsc{emp}’ co-occurs with a predicate featuring the perfect marker dɔ́n and the imperfective marker the morpheme ___. Sentence \REF{ex:key:743} additionally features the completive aspect{\fff} auxiliary verb fínis ‘finish (doing something)’, which adds even more emphatic force:

sentence: ___ yu nó bríng mí glás?
translation: ‘What, you haven’t brought (along) a glass for me?’
knowledge_point: The Spanish noun the morpheme ___ ‘its gloss ___’ is one of the most frequently employed secondary interjections and covers a large range of expressive meanings. It conveys real, playful, or mock surprise (\ref{ex:key:1644a}–\ref{ex:key:1644b}), shock and amazement \REF{ex:key:1644c}, awe and admiration \REF{ex:key:1644d}:

sentence: Yu gɛ́fɔ ___ tɔ́n=an.
translation: ‘You need to be stirring it.’
knowledge_point: We also encounter the imperfective marker in environments characterised by reduced finiteness{\fff}. Thus, the morpheme ___ optionally intervenes between certain aspectual auxiliaries (cf. \sectref{sec:6.4.1}) and modal verbs and the verbs that follow them (cf. \sectref{sec:10.5.3} for more the morpheme ___tails). Compare the following modal verbs gɛ́fɔ ‘have to’ \REF{ex:key:340} and wánt ‘want’ \REF{ex:key:341}:

sentence: A bin de chɛ́k sé a ___ máred.
translation: ‘I was thinking that I would marry/get married.’
knowledge_point: Future tense may be expressed explicitly by means of the potential mood marker the morpheme ___ \textsc{‘pot’.} The marker can be used indiscriminately with stative \REF{ex:key:386}, inchoative-stative (cf. máred ‘marry, be married’ in \ref{ex:key:390} below) and dynamic verbs \REF{ex:key:387}:

translation: ‘Get lost!’
knowledge_point: Given the right pragmatic context, the question word\is{question words} ús=sáy ‘\textsc{where’} may signal strong disagreement as well \REF{ex:key:659b}. The imperative\is{imperatives} clause the morpheme ___ dé ‘get lost’ can be employed to express strong and abusive disagreement \REF{ex:key:660b}:

sentence: Bɔt dá mɔní de ___ kwík.
translation: ‘But that money used to finish quickly.’
knowledge_point: The verb the morpheme ___ ‘its gloss ___’ expresses completive aspect. The use of the morpheme ___ as a lexical verb with the meaning ‘its gloss ___’ is exemplified in \REF{ex:key:362}:

sentence: Dɛn nó kin ___ sɛ́f.
translation: ‘They didn’t even use to know.’
knowledge_point: The habitual marker does not co-occur with the tense marker bin ‘\textsc{pst’} or the potential mood and future tense marker go ‘\textsc{pot’}. Like the imperfective marker de ‘\textsc{ipfv}’, kin ‘\textsc{hab}’ is itself unspecified for tense. Accordingly, sentence \REF{ex:key:345} above is translated as past habitual, because the time frame of the corresponding discourse context suggests so.\is{habitual aspect}

sentence: E ___ sé e kán yɛ́stadé.
translation: ‘It’s good that he came yesterday.’
knowledge_point: Evaluative verbs like the morpheme ___ ‘be its gloss ___’, gúd ‘be good’, or bád ‘be bad’ can induce either an indicative or a subjunctive mood over their complements. Evaluative verbs are followed by indicative complements when these are intended to convey factual information about present or past situations \REF{ex:key:1410}:

sentence: A ___ gó Alemania wán dé.
translation: ‘I absolutely have to go to Germany one day.’
knowledge_point: Alternatively, Pichi employs the two obligative mood markers fɔ ‘\textsc{prep}’ \REF{ex:key:416} and the morpheme ___ ‘\textsc{obl}’ (cf. \ref{ex:key:421} below) in order to express obligation. The marker fɔ may express both weak and strong obligation. The function of fɔ extends further to uses as a TMA marker to indicate counterfactual mood in the \textsc{then-}clause of conditionals\is{conditional clauses}, cf. the first and second occurrence of fɔ in \REF{ex:key:416}:

sentence: \'{A}fta di róp ___ wi nó sí nó mán wé e híb=an.
gloss: then DEF rope ___ 1PL NEG see NEG man SUB 3SG.SBJ throw=3SG.OBJ
translation: ‘And the rope, we didn’t see anybody who threw it.’
knowledge_point: For example, sentence \REF{ex:key:687} features the dislocated and topical object NP di róp ‘the rope’, followed by the focus particle the morpheme ___. In contrast to fronting (i.e. in question formation), the use of dislocation{\fff} comes along with the use of a resumptive pronoun{\fff} (here the \textsc{3sg.obj} pronoun =an) in the original object position of the left-dislocated constituent:

sentence: ___ nóto yu báy dán húman go bít yú sóté yu go gó lɛ́f=an.
gloss: ___ NEG.FOC 2SG buy that woman POT beat 2SG.INDP until 2SG POT go leave=3SG.OBJ
translation: ‘If it’s not that [the correct type] you’ve bought, that woman would beat you until you would go return it.’
knowledge_point: Nóto sé ‘it’s not that’ always signals contrastive focus of a clause or sentence \REF{ex:key:711}. In \REF{ex:key:712}, a conditional clause is singled out for focus. Hence, the negative focus marker nóto appears after the morpheme ___ ‘its gloss ___’:

sentence: Síns ___ a bí pikín, a de mɛ́mba fɔ kɔmɔ́t na dí kɔ́ntri.
gloss: since ___ 1SG.SBJ BE child 1SG.SBJ IPFV think.of PREP go.out LOC this country
translation: ‘Since I was a child, I think about leaving this country.’
knowledge_point: The preposition síns ‘since’ is one of two dedicated temporal prepositions of Pichi (the other one being ápás ‘after’, cf. \sectref{sec:8.2.2}) and may introduce source clauses in combination with the subordinator the morpheme ___ ‘\textsc{sub’,} cf. \REF{ex:key:1519} below:

sentence: Yu ___ bɔ́n fo pikín, (...)
translation: ‘You have given birth to four children, (...)’
knowledge_point: The negation of the perfect tense-aspect is asymmetrical. While the affirmative features the marker the morpheme ___ ‘\textsc{prf}’ \REF{ex:key:541}, the negative perfect is formed with a suppletive allomorph, i.e. either of the free variants nɛ́a and nɔ́ba ‘\textsc{neg.prf}’ \REF{ex:key:542}:

sentence: Wé yu go fɔdɔ́n yu go ___ bád.
translation: ‘When you fall you’ll be in a bad state.’
knowledge_point: Predicate adjective clauses may be marked for \textsc{TMA} like any other copula clause featuring the copula the morpheme ___. Compare the adjective bád ‘ill’ in \REF{ex:key:836} with a future tens\is{future tense}e reference:

sentence: Di strít ___ dé wɔwɔ́.
translation: ‘The street is too messed up.’
knowledge_point: In \REF{ex:key:521}, the morpheme ___ ‘its gloss ___ (much)’ occurs before the stative verb évi ‘be heavy’. In \REF{ex:key:522}, the morpheme ___ appears before the locative-existential copula dé:

sentence: Dí ___ a de gó Lubá.
translation: ‘This Wednesday, I am going to Luba.’
knowledge_point: Most speakers are not familiar with Pichi day names and employ the Spanish day nomenclature \REF{ex:key:1746}. Even older speakers rarely if ever use the corresponding Pichi day names mɔ́nde ‘Monday’, tyúsde ‘Tuesday’, wɛ́nsde ‘its gloss ___’, tɔsde ‘Thursday’, frayde ‘Friday’, sátidé ‘Saturday’, and sɔ́nde ‘Sunday’ \REF{ex:key:1747}:

sentence: A ték papá ___ bɛ́g=an.
translation: ‘I implored him in the name of God.’
knowledge_point: In the first type, the object of the V1 ték ‘take’ is the instrument\is{instrument SVC}\index{} or means used for performing V2. Compare wán blák lapá ‘a black cloth’ in \REF{ex:key:1561}. The instrument may also be an abstract noun like páwa ‘power’ \REF{ex:key:1562} or papá the morpheme ___ ‘its gloss ___’ in the idiom in \REF{ex:key:1563}:

sentence: ___ wé, a nó go kán.
translation: ‘No way, I won’t come.’
knowledge_point: Even stronger disagreement is expressed through the negative phrases the morpheme ___ wán dé ‘never’ \REF{ex:key:657b} and the morpheme ___ wé ‘no way’ \REF{ex:key:658b}. The following two sentence pairs illustrate their use in signalling disagreement in response to a question:

sentence: Sé dɛn ___ dɛn sɛ́f ɔ fɔ lɛk háw dɛn bɛ́n dɛn sɛ́f?
gloss: QUOT 3PL ___ 3PL self or PREP like how 3PL bend 3PL self
translation: ‘That they’re leaning (onto something) or how they’re stooped over?’
knowledge_point: The basic posture verbs slíp ‘lie (down), sleep’, tínap ‘stand (up)’ and sidɔ́n ‘sit (down)’ are never encountered with a reflexive pronoun in the corpus (cf. \sectref{sec:8.1.3} for an extensive treatment). In contrast, verbs denoting less prototypical postures, e.g. the morpheme ___ ‘its gloss ___ over’ and bɛ́n ‘bend (over)’ in (\ref{ex:key:1303}–\ref{ex:key:1304}), as well as those denoting other types of body-related events, e.g. háyd ‘hide’ in (\ref{ex:key:1305}–\ref{ex:key:1306}) are found with or without reflexive pronouns:

sentence: Dɛn de sláp ___ sɛ́f.
translation: ‘They’re slapping each other.’
knowledge_point: Next to its use as a reflexive anaphor, the pronominal sɛ́f ‘self’ also serves as a reciprocal pronominal with plural referents. In sentence \REF{ex:key:1232}, the reciprocal NP is an object to the verb sláp ‘slap’, in \REF{ex:key:1233} to the locative noun bifó ‘before’:

sentence: Háw e bin só, ___ e bigín, háw e salút yú?
gloss: how 3SG.SBJ PST show ___ 3SG.SBJ begin how 3SG.SBJ greet 2SG.INDP
translation: ‘How did he show [respect], how did he begin, how did he greet you?’
knowledge_point: A second and equally common means of questioning manner adverbials is provided by the monomorphemic question word the morpheme ___ ‘its gloss ___’. Sentence \REF{ex:key:631} involves a main clause, example \REF{ex:key:632} a main and a subordinate clause:

sentence: Wán ___ watá.
translation: ‘One glass of water’
knowledge_point: In the associative construction, two nouns are juxtaposed, whereby the “possessor” (the modifier noun) modifies the “possessed” noun (the modified noun). Firstly, this construction is always employed when the possessor is instantiated in a possessive pronoun. Secondly, associative constructions express various relations of modification, either exclusively or in complementarity with compounds (cf. \sectref{sec:4.4}). One relation of modification that is always expressed as an associative construction if the possessor is not a multi-constituent NP is a “measure/entity” relation \REF{ex:key:237}. In such constructions, the modifier noun is the measure (the morpheme ___ ‘its gloss ___’) and the modified noun the entity measured (watá ‘water’): \is{associative constructions}

sentence: Wé e bin dɔ́n ___ gó, e tɛ́l mí sé di tín wé e fít gí mi, e wánt lɛ́f mi sɔn ríng.
gloss: SUB 3SG.SBJ PST PRF ___ go 3SG.SBJ tell 1SG.INDP QUOT DEF thing SUB 3SG.SBJ can give 1SG.INDP 3SG.SBJ want leave 1SG.INDP some ring
translation: ‘When he was just about to go, he told me that the thing he could give me, he wanted to leave me a ring.’
knowledge_point: In the corpus, the maximal number of TMA markers encountered in one clause is three (e.g. \ref{ex:key:402}). The markers bin ‘\textsc{pst}’, go ‘\textsc{pot}’, and kin ‘\textsc{hab’} are mutually exclusive. The imperfective marker the morpheme ___ has the withe morpheme ___st distribution and co-occurs with all markers except fɔ ‘\textsc{cond’}. In contrast, the narrative perfective marker kán has a far more restricted distribution. It only co-occurs with bin ‘\textsc{pst’}, and it does so only in two instances in the corpus. Iterative aspect, expressed by reduplication, is most compatible with the imperfective senses expressed by the morpheme ___ ‘\textsc{ipfv’} and kin ‘\textsc{hab’}, but it is also compatible with the tense/mood markers bin ‘\textsc{pst’} and gó ‘\textsc{pot’}. The imperfective aspect harmonises with the habitual aspect. When the morpheme ___ ‘\textsc{ipfv}’ and kin ‘\textsc{hab}’ co-occur, there is no additional composite sense. The co-occurrence of subjunctive mék ‘\textsc{sbjv’} and imperfective the morpheme ___ ‘\textsc{ipfv’} is very rare in the corpus.

sentence: A ___ pút=an pantáp mi bɛlɛ́.
translation: ‘I (took him and) put him onto my belly.’
knowledge_point: Compare the alternative translations of \REF{ex:key:1564} and \REF{ex:key:1565}. Note the use of a resumptive\is{resumptive pronouns} object pronoun alone in the first example, and the use of both a resumptive object and subject pronoun in the second one:

sentence: A wáka ___ fút.
translation: ‘I walked by foot.’
knowledge_point: The role of instrument is expressed through the morpheme ___ ‘its gloss ___’ if instruments \REF{ex:key:1065}, materials \REF{ex:key:1066}, and functions \REF{ex:key:1067} are involved. Instruments and materials can also be expressed by argument-introducing SVCs involving ték ‘take’ (cf. \sectref{sec:9.1.4}):

sentence: Sí, na ___ mí sɛ́f kin dé.
translation: ‘See, it’s like that that I’m also usually like.’
knowledge_point: There are also numerous instances of focused adverbs. Compare the adverb the morpheme ___ ‘so, like this’ in \REF{ex:key:704}, which is often encountered in a cleft construction na the morpheme ___ ‘it’s like that, that’s how it is’, as well as focused dé ‘there’ \REF{ex:key:705}:

sentence: Ɔ́l Ghána bɔ́y-s ___ wé dɛn dé (...)
translation: ‘All the Ghanaian guys that were around (...)’
knowledge_point: Finally, I point out that Pichi has at least two nouns with suppletive plural forms which are occasionally employed instead of the regular plural involving the morpheme ___ ‘\textsc{pl’}. The relevant singular-plural pairs are gál-gáls ‘girl-girls’ and bɔ́y-bɔ́ys ‘boy-boys’. However, these forms are not suppletive in the true sense, since they feature the segmentable but only marginally productive plural morpheme \{-s\}, which is only attested with these two nouns. As example \REF{ex:key:217} above shows, these forms may also be followed by the pluraliser the morpheme ___.\is{number!nouns}

sentence: Sé “ús=tín kin ___ ínsay dé?”
translation: ‘(They) said “what is usually in there?”‘
knowledge_point: Human propensities are divided between inchoative-stative (e.g. gudhát ‘be good-hearted’, wíkɛd ‘be wicked’, badhát ‘be mean’, klɛ́va ‘be clever’) and dynamic verbs (e.g. gládin ‘be glad’, jɛ́lɔs ‘be envious’) according to whether they denote intrinsic or transient properties. Resultatives{\fff} are exclusively expressed through the stative readings of labile change-of-state verbs (e.g. brók ‘break, be broken’, chɛ́r ‘tear, be torn’, lɔ́s ‘lose, be lost’ and wɛ́r ‘be dressed’). Semantic types like position or location are expressed through other means, such as copula clauses featuring the locative-existential copula the morpheme ___ (cf. e.g. \ref{ex:key:793}–\ref{ex:key:794}) in combination with adverbials, or through locative verbs like {\fff}lé ‘lie’ and tínap ‘stand (up)’ (cf. \sectref{sec:8.1.3}).

sentence: Bueno aunque dé, bɔkú ___ económico dé.
gloss: good although there much ___ economic BE.LOC
translation: ‘Alright although there, there’s a lot of economic interest.’
knowledge_point: Copula clauses\is{copula!locative-existential} featuring dé \textsc{‘be.loc’} typically acquire an existential reading when they lack a copula complement\is{complements!copula complements}. In these clauses, we find the predicated entity, which may be of varying complexity, in the subject position \REF{ex:key:808}. Since there is no complement to provide further specification, the clause acquires the default locative and manner reading that typifies such dé{}-clauses \REF{ex:key:809}:

sentence: Ɛ́ni sáy wé pɔ́sin ___ sidɔ́n, dɛn de sidɔ́n.
gloss: every side SUB person ___ stay 3PL IPFV stay
translation: ‘Anywhere that a person wanted to stay, they stayed.’
knowledge_point: Present tense\is{present tense} is not expressed by means of elements specialised to this function. Instead, present tense reference is established by default through a variety of means. Bare stative verbs (cf. \ref{ex:key:315}) and in the appropriate context inchoative-stative verbs \REF{ex:key:316} are assigned present tense by default when marked for factative\is{factative TMA} TMA. Present tense reference is also established with inchoative-stative verbs via the use of the imperfective aspec\is{imperfective aspect}t marker de (cf. \ref{ex:key:336}) and with both lexical aspect classes by the use of the habitual\is{habitual aspect} marker kin (cf. \ref{ex:key:344}–\ref{ex:key:345}). Dynamic verbs are assigned present tense by default when they appear with the imperfective marker de (cf. \ref{ex:key:329}) and the habitual aspect marker kin (cf. \ref{ex:key:342}).

sentence: Porque e fíba sé di gɛ́l [wé e bin de ték ___ e bin gɛ́t bɔkú bɔ́y dɛn.
gloss: because 3SG.SBJ seem QUOT DEF girl SUB 3SG.SBJ PST IPFV take ___ 3SG.SBJ PST get much boy PL
translation: ‘Because it seems that the girl that he was going out with, she had many boyfriends.’
knowledge_point: Example \REF{ex:key:1567} above is also noteworthy because it shows what happens when the object of ték is relativised. The object di gɛ́l ‘the girl’ is placed in the head noun position, while the relativised position may remain empty, which leads to V1 and V2 occurring next to each other. Contiguity of ték and the V2 is also found when the object of ték is fronted in content questions{\fff}. Sentence \REF{ex:key:1568} features the questioned concrete noun plɛ́nk ‘board’ and \REF{ex:key:1569} the abstract noun stáyl ‘manner’:

sentence: \'{U}s=tín de mék ___ mék yu nó wók tidé?
gloss: Q=thing IPFV make ___ SBJV 2SG NEG work today
translation: ‘What is causing you not to work today?’
knowledge_point: Sentence \REF{ex:key:649} below contains the most verb-like instance of mék. Here, mék ‘make’ not only functions as a main verb to the complement verb wók ‘work’. It also induces a subjunctive\is{subjunctive mood} mood over the complement clause, because it is employed with its lexical meaning as a deontic causative verb (cf. \sectref{sec:9.4.4})\is{causative constructions}. Equally, the main verb mék is fully finite as can be seen by the presence of the imperfective marker de ‘\textsc{ipfv}’:

sentence: Nó mɔs ___ dán sáy!
translation: ‘(You) must not go to that place!’
knowledge_point: Prohibitive\is{prohibitives} clauses featuring mɔs ‘\textsc{obl}’ are formed like regular negative imperatives\is{imperatives} without a \textsc{2sg} personal pronoun \REF{ex:key:423}:

sentence: Di tín de gó ___ bád.
translation: ‘The matter is going bad for me.’
knowledge_point: Now consider the transitive use of fáyn in the following two sentences. Note that a transitive use may also lead to an idiosyncratic meaning of fáyn. Sentence \REF{ex:key:1121} presents the regular, derived transitive meaning of ‘make beautiful’, while \REF{ex:key:1122} represents a case of idiomatic transitivity with a “dative of interest” reading of the experiencer\is{experiencer} object pronoun of fáyn. Such a meaning is also recorded for cases of idiomatic transitivity with other verbs low on the transitivity scale, e.g. the motion verbs\is{motion verbs} gó ‘go’ \REF{ex:key:1085}, rɔ́n ‘run’ \REF{ex:key:1087}, and sube ‘rise, raise’ \REF{ex:key:1108}:

sentence: ___ dé sé dán gál e bin de kán yá.
gloss: ___ BE.LOC QUOT that girl 3SG.SBJ PST IPFV come here
translation: ‘It’s that/it came to pass that that girl used to come here.’

In such factivthe morpheme ___ clausthe morpheme ___s, ththe morpheme ___ copula vthe morpheme ___rb takthe morpheme ___s a dummy noun\is{dummy nouns} likthe morpheme ___ tín ‘thing’, kés ‘mattthe morpheme ___r’, or ththe morpheme ___ the morpheme ___xplthe morpheme ___tivthe morpheme ___ subjthe morpheme ___ct\is{the morpheme ___xplthe morpheme ___tivthe morpheme ___} pronoun the morpheme ___ ‘\tthe morpheme ___xtsc{3sg.sbj}’. Factivthe morpheme ___ main clausthe morpheme ___s likthe morpheme ___ ththe morpheme ___ onthe morpheme ___ in \REF{the morpheme ___x:kthe morpheme ___y:1409} arthe morpheme ___ vthe morpheme ___ry common as introductory formulas in narrativthe morpheme ___ discoursthe morpheme ___ (cf. also \rthe morpheme ___f{the morpheme ___x:kthe morpheme ___y:1136}):

sentence: Dí miércoles a de ___ Lubá.
translation: ‘This Wednesday, I’m going to Luba.’
knowledge_point: In contrast to wáka ‘walk’ and fláy ‘fly’, other motion verbs\is{motion verbs} like the morpheme ___ ‘its gloss ___’ can appear in transitive clauses, in which the its gloss ___al is expressed as an object. This is particularly so when the its gloss ___al object is a named place. Compare the object Lubá ‘(the town of) Luba’ in \REF{ex:key:1084}:

sentence: Bɔt di pé wé yu gɛ́fɔ pé, if yu nó de gí mí yu fɔ́s ___ [wé na in gí yú dí bɛlɛ́], yu de gí mi di pikín [wé de kɔmɔ́t].
gloss: but DEF pay SUB 2SG have.to pay if 2SG NEG IPFV give 1SG.INDP 2SG first ___ SUB FOC 3SG.INDP give 2SG.INDP this belly 2SG IPFV give 1SG.INDP DEF child SUB IPFV come.out
translation: ‘But the price that you have to pay (is), if you don’t give me your first man, who it is him who gave you the first pregnancy, you will give me the child that will come out.’
knowledge_point: Pichi exhibits generous possibilities of relative clause formation (cf. \citealt[148]{Keenan1985}). For example, the relativisation of a nominal that is part of a coordinate structure is permitted \REF{ex:key:1426}. Equally, a relative clause may contain a focused resumptive pronoun\is{resumptive pronouns} \REF{ex:key:1427}:

sentence: Bɔt ín sidɔ́n ___ dɔ́n dɔ́n yandá.
translation: ‘But he stays far down over there.’
knowledge_point: Repetition produces a range of emphatic, intensifying nuances. The core meaning of repetition is augmentative, hence an iconic “more of the same”. However, the expression of plural number does not lie within the functional range of repetition. In the following three examples, we witness the use of intensifying repetition for emphasis with the temporal adverb náw ‘now’ \REF{ex:key:146}, the locative noun the morpheme ___ ‘its gloss ___’ \REF{ex:key:147}, the common noun fámbul ‘family’, and the attributively used property item bɔkú ‘(be) much’ \REF{ex:key:148}:

sentence: Wé e ___ kɔmɔ́t wók, a kin mék=an so, lɛk háw mún fínis.
gloss: SUB 3SG.SBJ ___ come.out work 1SG.SBJ HAB make=3SG.OBJ like.that like how month finish
translation: ‘When he comes from work/ when he has just finished working, I do like this to him [stretches out hand], as soon as the month is over.’
knowledge_point: In other instances, the meaning of kɔmɔ́t is intermediary between a spatial and a more grammatical sense. In \REF{ex:key:356}, it is the presence of the locative question word ús=sáy ‘where’ that creates ambiguity between the literal and the egressive senses of kɔmɔ́t. In sentence \REF{ex:key:357}, semantic ambiguity is produced by the presence of wók which may mean ‘work’ (the noun) or ‘to work’ (the verb). If the former translation is preferred, wók is analysed as the (source) object of kɔmɔ́t. With the latter translation wók is a complement verb:

sentence: Na ín ___ dán húman dɔ́n de wók fɔ.
gloss: FOC 3SG.INDP ___ that woman PRF IPFV work PREP
translation: ‘It is only that that that woman is working for.’
knowledge_point: Compound pronouns feature a personal pronoun and the quantifiers\is{quantifiers} tú ‘two’ and/or ɔ́l ‘all’. They are formed by the same means as other compounds: The lexical H tone of the initial component(s) is erased and replaced by an L tone while the final component retains its lexically assigned H tone. Evidence that compounding is indeed at work in the formation of compound pronouns comes from (\ref{ex:key:289}–\ref{ex:key:291}) above. The presence of the postposed quantifiers wán ‘alone’ and the morpheme ___ ‘its gloss ___’ in these examples requires the use of H-toned emphatic personal pronouns. In contrast, the \textsc{3pl} form of the personal pronoun in \REF{ex:key:293} below is L-toned, although the quantifier ɔ́l ‘all’ is in the same syntactic position as wán and the morpheme ___ in (\ref{ex:key:289}–\ref{ex:key:291}) above.\is{number!pronouns}

sentence: Entonces wán problema diplomático kán dé entre ___ wet Gabón.
gloss: so one problem diplomatic PFV BE.LOC between ___ with PLACE
translation: ‘So a diplomatic problem came to be between Guinea and Gabon.’
knowledge_point: Other semantic fields characterised by a high incidence of codemixing involve formalised, institutional domains. One of the few Pichi country names in use is Panyá ‘Spain’, the designation for the former colonial power. Spanish lexemes are exclusively employed for country names like Guinea (Ecuatorial) ‘Equatorial Guinea’, Gabón ‘Gabon’ \REF{ex:key:1754}, ethnonyms like europeo ‘European’ or cameruneses ‘Cameroonians’ \REF{ex:key:1755}, as well as terms belonging to the state domain such as problema diplomático ‘diplomatic problem’ \REF{ex:key:1754}:

sentence: A nó mánech ___ tidé.
translation: ‘I didn’t manage to meet her today.’
knowledge_point: The verbs hébul ‘be capable’ \REF{ex:key:407} and mánech ‘be capable, manage’ \REF{ex:key:408} are usually employed to express capacity rather than ability:

sentence: Sé ín nó ___ {in} {abuelo} skrách=an.
translation: ‘(He) said, he [EMP] didn’t want his grandfather to scratch him.’
knowledge_point: Notwithstanding the absence of the subjunctive marker, I analyse the clauses in bold in \REF{ex:key:1403} and \REF{ex:key:1404} above as subjunctive clauses. Evidence comes from the reduced TMA marking that characterises these clauses. Although both subordinate clauses are future-referring, they are not marked by go ‘\textsc{pot}’ as they would if they occurred in main clauses or clauses with independent time reference (e.g. in quotative clause\is{quotative clauses}s introduced by sé ‘\textsc{quot}’). Instead, the subordinate verbs gó ‘go’ and skrách ‘scratch’ appear stripped of any TMA marking as do subjunctive complements introduced by mék ‘\textsc{sbjv}’.\is{deontic modality}

sentence: Yu nó fít jɔ́s trowé di tín ___ na strít só.
gloss: 2SG NEG can just throw.away DEF thing ___ LOC street like.that
translation: ‘You can’t just throw the things into the street like that.’
knowledge_point: Pichi marks plural number via the postposed pluraliser\is{pluraliser} the morpheme ___ which is identical to the \textsc{3pl} dependent pronoun. The pluraliser is clitic-like in one respect: It may not be separated from the noun it refers to by any constituent. Typically, the pluraliser occurs with count nouns \REF{ex:key:207}, but it may also follow collective nouns like pípul ‘people’ \REF{ex:key:208}: \is{cliticisation}

sentence: Di glás ___ di domɔ́t.
translation: ‘The glass is near the door.’
knowledge_point: The locative nouns the morpheme ___ ‘its gloss ___’, kɔ́na ‘next to’, nadó ‘outside’, and bifó ‘before, front’ are not normally found as complements to na ‘\textsc{loc}’ in prepositional phrases\is{prepositional phrases} like the ones above. The peculiar distribution of the morpheme ___ and kɔ́na may be due to their multifunctionality. Nía also functions as a locative verb ‘be its gloss ___’ (cf. \ref{ex:key:939}), kɔ́na as a common noun ‘corner’, and bifó as a time clause linker ‘before’ (cf. \sectref{sec:10.7.3}). In \REF{ex:key:933} below, kɔ́na is employed as a locative noun, in the following example \REF{ex:key:916}, as a common noun:

sentence: Náw fɔ mék dɛn fít gɛ́t wán amiga nadó wé yu sísta ___ sabí, in go had.
gloss: now PREP SBJV 3PL can get one girlfriend outside SUB 2SG sister ___ know 3SG.INDP POT be.hard
translation: ‘Now for them to be able to have a girl-friend outside while/although your sisters know, that will be difficult.’
knowledge_point: The boundary is fuzzy between temporal and other adverbial meanings of clauses introduced by wé. In \REF{ex:key:1463}, the temporal sense of the wé{}-clause shades off into a manner or circumstance sense. Context may also give rise to a concessive\is{concessive clauses} meaning of the subordinate clause \REF{ex:key:1464}:

sentence: Di ___ dé sé, mék e mék rabia wet mí.
gloss: DEF ___ BE.LOC QUOT SBJV 3SG.SBJ make anger with 1SG.INDP
translation: ‘The thing is let her be angry with me.’
knowledge_point: The quotative marker also introduces the complements of copula verbs in statements of facts. In such factive clauses, the copula verb takes a dummy noun\is{dummy nouns} like the morpheme ___ ‘its gloss ___’, kés ‘matter’, or the expletive subject\is{expletive} pronoun e ‘\textsc{3sg.sbj}’. Factive main clauses like the one in \REF{ex:key:1409} are very common as introductory formulas in narrative discourse (cf. also \ref{ex:key:1136}):

sentence: A nó bin fít tɔ́k, bikɔs a nó fít ___ a kán a de lúk yú.
gloss: 1SG.SBJ NEG PST can talk because 1SG.SBJ NEG can ___ 1SG.SBJ come 1SG.SBJ IPFV look 2SG.INDP
translation: ‘I couldn’t talk, because I couldn’t talk, I came (and) was just looking at you.’
knowledge_point: Pichi has a three-way distinction of ability. The modal verb fít ‘can’ expresses ability in a general sense, but it does not normally cover mental ability \REF{ex:key:406}:

sentence: A ___ na Malábo.
translation: ‘I reside in Malabo.’
knowledge_point: The ground associated with the intransitive stative verb the morpheme ___ ‘its gloss ___’ may only be expressed as a prepositional phrase (\ref{ex:key:1093}–\ref{ex:key:1094}):

sentence: Mí ___ dé dé, a bin mék dásɔl, dís, a de mék} fínga dɛn, manicura.
gloss: 1SG.INDP ___ BE.LOC there 1SG.SBJ PST make only this 1SG.SBJ IPFV make finger PL manicure
translation: ‘(As for) me, (when) I was there, I only made, this, I used to make fingers, manicure.’
knowledge_point: Sentence \REF{ex:key:381} above is part of an orienting section of a narrative and provides background information to a story. The stative copula dé and the first dynamic verb (marked by superscript as \textsuperscript{1}mek ‘make’) are overtly marked for past tense with the morpheme ___. Once the use of the morpheme ___ with these two verbs has anchored the sentence (and in fact, the entire following narrative) in the past, overt past tense marking is unnecessary with subsequent verbs as is the case with the second dynamic verb (marked by superscript as \textsuperscript{2}mek in \ref{ex:key:381}).

sentence: Ɔ́l Ghána bɔ́y-s ___ wé dɛn dé (...)
translation: ‘All the Ghanaian guys that were around (...)’
knowledge_point: The pluraliser is also consistently made use of with inserted Spanish nouns marked with the Spanish plural morpheme \{-s\} \REF{ex:key:216}. The same is true of the few instances in the corpus, in which the nouns bɔ́y ‘boy’ and gál ‘girl’ are marked for plural with the marginal Pichi plural morpheme \{-s\} as in \REF{ex:key:217}:

sentence: Pikín náw, ___ nó hád.
translation: ‘As for [having] kids, that’s not difficult.’

knowledge_point: Imperatives \REF{ex:key:538} are negated either with a symmetrical structure \REF{ex:key:539} or with an asymmetrical structure involving a negative subjunctive\is{subjunctive mood} clause \REF{ex:key:540}:

knowledge_point: The Spathe morpheme ___sh coordinator pair the morpheme ___ – the morpheme ___ ‘its gloss ___ – nor, not even’ can express negative disjunction in Pichi utterances. Like in Spathe morpheme ___sh, the morpheme ___ can be used alone \REF{ex:key:1730} or in discontinuous negation\is{negation} \REF{ex:key:1731}. Unlike in Spathe morpheme ___sh, however, subject disjunction in Pichi requires the kind of negative concord characteristic of other negative clauses in Pichi \REF{ex:key:1731}:

However, ús=káyn is not found in conjunction with human-denoting generic nouns like mán ‘man’ or pɔ́sin ‘person’ with the meaning of ‘\textsc{who’.}

knowledge_point: Other phrasal interjections are employed to seek attention, approbation and confirmation. The phrases the morpheme ___ tɔ́k ‘don’t talk’, which appears together with nɔ́ and ɛ́n in \REF{ex:key:655} further above, and the morpheme ___ láf ‘\textsc{neg} laugh’ = ‘I’m not kidding’ \REF{ex:key:1660b} underline the credibility of the speaker’s proposition or story. A similar function is fulfilled by a tɛ́l yú ‘I tell you’ in \REF{ex:key:1661}:

knowledge_point: Besithe morpheme ___s its use for expressing aspectual relations, the functions of the morpheme ___ reach into the domain of modality and overlap with those of the potential marker go ‘\textsc{pot’}. The imperfective marker may express future tense in combination with an appropriate time adverbial \REF{ex:key:338}. It can also express conditional modality in \textsc{then-}clauses and hypothetical statements contingent upon inferred conditions \REF{ex:key:339}:\is{conditional clauses}

knowledge_point: Alternatively, Pichi employs the two obligative mood markers fɔ ‘\textsc{prep}’ \REF{ex:key:416} and mɔs ‘\textsc{obl}’ (cf. \ref{ex:key:421} below) in order to express obligation. The marker fɔ may express both weak and strong obligation. The function of fɔ extends further to uses as a TMA marker to indicate counterfactual mood in the \textsc{then-}clause of conditionals\is{conditional clauses}, cf. the first and second occurrence of fɔ in \REF{ex:key:416}:

knowledge_point: The objects of prepositions may also be questioned in situ or be fronted. When fronted, either the entire prepositional phrase appears at the beginning of the clause, or the preposition is stranded. However, stranding\is{stranding} in questions is only attested with fɔ ‘\textsc{prep}’ \REF{ex:key:594}, wet ‘with’ \REF{ex:key:595}, and pan ‘on’ \REF{ex:key:596}:
